examples.sentence: Marie fait lire ce livre aux enfants.

derivationStages.stageRecord: On this reading, Marie makes the children read this book. The analysis uses an IP-based version of X-bar theory: Marie occupies the matrix subject position, and the children initially occupy the subject position of a defective infinitival IP selected by faire. Lire assigns its Agent role to that embedded subject and its Theme role to ce livre; faire assigns the Causer role to Marie and selects the reading eventuality. The infinitival subject has no Case yet. Its determiner is represented as les, without a surface-token association, because the eventual aux realizes both a dative marker and this determiner. Fait is introduced as the lexically inflected form of faire, following a lexicalist treatment of inflection; its subsequent movement to finite I does not change its spelling. The infinitive has no independent finite tense or CP boundary.
derivationStages.statement: Establish the underlying causative structure with the children as the readers.

values.condition: the infinitive has a direct object

derivationStages.stageRecord: The reading VP raises from the complement of infinitival I and adjoins to the defective embedded IP. Its trace remains in the earlier complement position. This predicate-fronting implementation of faire-infinitif places lire ce livre before the embedded subject without lowering that subject or moving the book independently. Causative restructuring makes the defective domain transparent for the Case configuration: the direct object receives accusative, while the overt subject of this transitive infinitive receives dative. A non-thematic à shell expresses that dative around the existing subject DP; it does not introduce a recipient role. Finally, à and les jointly realize aux. These commitments distinguish this analysis from a reading in which aux enfants is an argument of lire.
derivationStages.statement: Derive infinitive–object–causee order and realize the dative causee.

derivationStages.stageRecord: The finite causative verb raises from matrix V to I, leaving a head trace. The earlier predicate fronting remains intact, so the pronounced sequence is Marie fait lire ce livre aux enfants. Finite I licenses nominative on Marie and checks third-person singular agreement. The resulting causative domain contains an accusative Theme and a dative causee, with the children retaining the Agent role assigned in their underlying subject position. This is a trace analysis, not an analysis with pronounced lower copies. Neither the name nor the two lexical nominal descriptions require a binding dependency; the movement chains and Case relations supply the relevant GB licensing.
derivationStages.statement: Complete the finite clause on the causee reading.

examples.sentence: Marie fait lire ce livre aux enfants.

derivationStages.stageRecord: This analysis uses classical GB noun phrases, with determiners in the specifier position of NP, and a lexical-restructuring treatment of faire-infinitif. Marie is the causer, ce livre is the theme, and aux enfants will express the causee. The finite lexical form fait and the infinitive lire are initially separate heads. The abstract present-tense I head is unpronounced. Within the independently constructed PP, à and the plural article les jointly realize aux; neither morpheme independently corresponds to that whole input token. The contraction relation connects these two overt morphological contributors.
derivationStages.statement: Select the constituents for the reading in which the children are the readers.

values.clausalCommitment: one clause; no embedded IP or PRO

derivationStages.stageRecord: First, lexical argument composition combines faire and lire into one complex verbal head. This is the selected lexical-union analysis, not movement out of an independently projected infinitival clause: no embedded IP, PRO, or embedded subject trace is introduced. Because lire retains its direct-object theme, the construction realizes its reader argument as a dative causee rather than as a second accusative NP. The compound selects ce livre and the causee PP in a recursively expanded V′; the PP is a constructionally licensed argument, not a nominal modifier. The resulting VP combines with finite I, and Marie is base-generated in Spec-IP. The thematic relation then assigns Causer to Marie, Theme to ce livre, and Reader/Causee to the NP inside aux enfants. The previously established contraction remains unchanged.
derivationStages.statement: Construct the causative clause with a dative causee.

relations.relation: V-to-I head movement and antecedent government

values.emptyCategoryLicensing: local antecedent government of the head trace
values.operation: raise the causative complex to I

values.interpretation: Marie causes the children to read this book

derivationStages.stageRecord: The complex verbal head now raises from its previously represented VP-internal position to I, leaving a silent head trace. Under the selected restructuring analysis, lire accompanies faire as part of the already formed head; this is not a separate extraction of lire at this stage. The head chain is local, and its lower occurrence is antecedent-governed by the raised head. Finite I then licenses nominative Case and third-person singular agreement on Marie. The verbal chain licenses accusative Case on ce livre through its VP-internal position, while à licenses dative/oblique Case on the causee NP. These Case relations preserve the theta assignments established before movement. There are no anaphors, pronouns, or nominal movement chains requiring additional Binding Theory dependencies. The final pronunciation is exactly Marie fait lire ce livre aux enfants.
derivationStages.statement: Complete the finite causative derivation and license the overt arguments.

examples.sentence: सीता ने वे किताबें पढ़ी थीं।

derivationStages.stageRecord: External Merge combines the proper name सीता, treated as an atomic D, with the postpositional case head ने. The resulting K-labeled object is head-final. Separately, the demonstrative D वे merges with N किताबें, producing a D-labeled object meaning ‘those books’; किताबें supplies feminine plural nominal features. Bare Phrase Structure projects the selecting head's label without introducing separate bar-level categories. The remaining workspace contains the participial V पढ़ी, a silent transitive ergative v, a silent perfect Asp, the finite past auxiliary T थीं, and a silent declarative C. The two verbal forms enter as whole-word lexical items, so no morpheme segmentation or collective realization is assumed. The selected ergative v is phi-defective and does not independently transfer the object-containing domain before the agreement operations used below.
derivationStages.statement: Construct the ergative subject and demonstrative object, and select the remaining heads.

derivationStages.stageRecord: V first merges with the demonstrative object, yielding a head-final V-labeled constituent. This establishes the books as the theme of reading. Silent v then merges with that constituent, and the subject K phrase externally merges as v's specifier. This establishes सीता as the agent. The selected transitive ergative v licenses the subject's inherent ergative case, overtly expressed by ने. The subject therefore does not remain an active candidate for the finite nominative and phi-agreement dependency. The theme, agent, and ergative-licensing relations are recorded in that establishment order.
derivationStages.statement: Build the transitive predicate and introduce its ergative external argument.

values.surfaceDistinction: The participle expresses feminine agreement without an independent singular–plural contrast in this auxiliary construction.

values.case: unmarked direct case, analyzed as nominative

derivationStages.stageRecord: Silent perfect Asp merges above the v-labeled constituent and selects the participial predicate. In this analysis, participial agreement is mediated by Asp: the unmarked object controls agreement on पढ़ी, while the inherently case-valued ergative subject is inactive for this dependency. The participle expresses feminine agreement; its form in this auxiliary construction does not independently distinguish feminine singular from feminine plural. T थीं then merges above Asp. T agrees with the same feminine plural object, visibly expressing feminine plural agreement on the auxiliary, and licenses the object's unmarked direct case, analyzed here as nominative. These dependencies are possible because the selected phi-defective v does not seal off the object before agreement. The agreement relations are established in the order Asp agreement, T agreement, then direct-case valuation. Perfect Asp under past T supplies the past-perfect interpretation, ‘Sita had read those books.’ No verbal head movement is posited: the lexical participle and the overt T already occupy the required head-final positions.
derivationStages.statement: Add perfect aspect and past tense, establishing object-controlled verbal agreement.

values.selection: pronounce the higher copy; silence the lower copy

values.agreementIndependence: The ergative subject occupies the subject position, but the object remains the agreement controller.

derivationStages.stageRecord: Internal Merge takes the subject K phrase from its previously established v-specifier position and places a higher occurrence in the specifier of T. The entire case-marked phrase moves, so सीता and ने remain together. The movement relation links the higher occurrence to the lower occurrence; corresponding phrase and terminal occurrences share lineages. Copy pronunciation selects the higher occurrence and silences the lower occurrence, yielding the initial sequence सीता ने without duplicating either token. This movement satisfies T's subject-position requirement independently of T's object-controlled agreement: the raised ergative subject does not become the agreement controller. Finally, silent declarative C merges with the completed T-labeled constituent. All projections remain binary and head-final where a head combines with its complement. The pronounced terminals are exactly सीता ने वे किताबें पढ़ी थीं, in the supplied order; the sentence-final punctuation is not a separate supplied token.
derivationStages.statement: Raise the ergative subject and complete the declarative clause.

examples.sentence: 美咲が健に貸した本を友子が返した。

derivationStages.stageRecord: External Merge builds the clause meaning that Misaki lent something to Ken. The unpronounced nominal operator is first merged as the theme complement of the verbal stem 貸し. The goal phrase 健に is merged above that complement, and transitive little v introduces the agent 美咲が. All projections are labeled by their selecting heads rather than by stipulated bar levels; the ordered branches implement Japanese head-final order. Proper names are treated as nominal D objects, and their particles as K heads. Transitive v licenses accusative on the object operator. The relative clause therefore has an object dependency, not a subject or recipient gap. The stem's spelling extends across the supplied boundary between 貸 and した, so no whole-token association is yet assigned to it.
derivationStages.statement: Construct the relative clause's thematic domain.

values.operation: joint morphological and orthographic realization without syntactic head movement

derivationStages.stageRecord: Past T is externally merged above the relative v domain. T licenses nominative on 美咲 through its が-marked nominal, without requiring subject raising: this analysis does not give Japanese T an obligatory EPP feature. At morphological interpretation, the stem 貸し and past た jointly realize the supplied tokens 貸 and した. This association respects the authored stem and tense boundaries rather than treating した as an independent syntactic word. No syntactic verb movement is posited.
derivationStages.statement: Add relative-clause tense and establish the realization of 貸した.

values.interpretation: the book is the theme of lending

derivationStages.stageRecord: A silent relative C selects the previously constructed tense domain. Its operator feature triggers Internal Merge of the object operator to the relative-clause edge from the complement position already present in the preceding workspace. Movement is represented with an unpronounced operator at the edge and a trace at its original position, rather than with full copies. The relative clause is then adjoined to the external nominal head 本; asymmetric adjunction preserves the nominal label. The operator chain supplies the theme variable predicated of that head, yielding ‘the book that Misaki lent to Ken.’ A silent D provides a nominal argument without imposing an overt article's definiteness specification, and を is merged as its K head. Its matrix accusative licensing awaits the matrix transitive domain.
derivationStages.statement: Close the object relative and construct the case-marked book phrase.

derivationStages.stageRecord: The complete book phrase is externally merged as the theme complement of the matrix stem 返し. Transitive little v then introduces 友子が as the returning agent. This establishes a canonical subject–object–verb thematic configuration before the object's later displacement; the supplied object-before-subject order is not built in by reversing their thematic positions. Matrix v licenses accusative on the book nominal, realized by を. The return predicate is used transitively without an additional syntactically projected recipient: the sentence does not state to whom Tomoko returned the book, and Ken's role inside the relative clause does not grammatically determine that recipient.
derivationStages.statement: Merge the book argument into the matrix predicate and introduce Tomoko.

values.operation: joint morphological and orthographic realization without syntactic head movement

derivationStages.stageRecord: Past T selects the matrix v domain and licenses nominative on 友子 through が. As in the relative clause, no EPP-driven subject movement is required, so Tomoko remains in the thematic subject position. The matrix stem 返し and past た receive their joint realization as the supplied tokens 返 and した. The workspace now contains a finite clause in which the case-licensed book phrase is still visibly the complement of the matrix verb. This intermediate structure fixes the source of the subsequent scrambling dependency.
derivationStages.statement: Establish matrix tense and the pre-scrambling finite clause.

values.interpretation: the displaced book argument remains the theme of returning

derivationStages.stageRecord: Internal Merge displaces the entire を-marked book phrase from the matrix verb's complement to the left edge of the matrix tense domain, above the in-situ subject 友子が. This is clause-internal object scrambling, not extraction from the relative clause and not a separate topic construction: を remains the object's case marker. The movement dependency uses a trace representation. The original complement occurrence is reduced to an unpronounced K trace; the landing occurrence contains the moved nominal and case head, including the intact relative clause. The chain preserves the book's theme interpretation and accusative licensing at its source. A silent declarative C then closes the sentence. The resulting pronounced order is exactly 美咲が健に貸した本を友子が返した, with both stem–tense associations retained. The written full stop marks sentence closure and is not an additional token in the supplied list. The completed interpretation is that Tomoko returned the book that Misaki had lent to Ken.
derivationStages.statement: Scramble the matrix object and complete the declarative sentence.

derivationStages.stageRecord: Lexical access and External Merge construct three head-final nominal objects. Proper names and the bare nominal 책 are treated as nominal arguments without additional silent determiner structure. The particle 는 marks 민수 as a topic; it is not analyzed as an overt nominative marker. The particle 에게 marks the recipient, and 을 marks the theme. Three morphological realization relations establish that each nominal and its particle jointly realize one supplied token. The verb 주 remains a separate syntactic object. Projection labels throughout identify the projecting head in Bare Phrase Structure; repeated labels do not introduce stipulated bar levels. This derivation takes 민수는 to be the overt thematic subject that subsequently moves to the clause's topic edge, rather than an independently generated hanging topic associated with an additional null subject.
derivationStages.statement: Construct the topic-marked subject, dative recipient, accusative theme, and lexical verb.

derivationStages.stageRecord: The verb first merges with the accusative theme. A silent applicative head then merges with that verbal object and introduces the dative recipient, giving the recipient a position above the theme. This is an applicative analysis of the Korean ditransitive, not an analysis in which 영희에게 modifies 책. A silent transitive little-v head merges with the applicative constituent, and the topic-marked subject is externally merged at its edge. The thematic relation identifies 민수 as Agent, 영희 as Goal, and 책 as Theme. Structural accusative licensing is then established between transitive little-v and the theme's case layer. The topic particle does not itself discharge the subject's structural Case requirement. No verb movement is needed to obtain the head-final order.
derivationStages.statement: Build the head-final giving predicate and merge its thematic subject.

values.operation: suffixal realization without syntactic head movement

derivationStages.stageRecord: The nonfinite linker 지 merges above the agentive predicate, and the negative auxiliary 않 selects the resulting constituent. The linker is analyzed as a dependent verbal functional head, not as an independent finite complementizer. Its complement remains transparent to the later licensing and raising of the thematic subject; no second external argument or controlled subject is introduced. Morphological suffixation associates 주 and 지 with the token 주지 while preserving them as distinct syntactic heads. The negative auxiliary takes scope over the giving-event description, including its recipient and theme. This yields denial of the giving event rather than constituent negation of 책 or 영희. The auxiliary stem has not yet received its finite realization.
derivationStages.statement: Construct the long-form negative auxiliary predicate.

relations.relation: subject Internal Merge and copy pronunciation

values.movement: A-movement to the finite subject position
values.pronunciation: higher occurrence pronounced; thematic occurrence silent

derivationStages.stageRecord: Past T merges with the negative auxiliary constituent, placing tense above negation. Finite T licenses the structural nominative Case of the nominal inside the topic-marked subject; Korean supplies no overt agreement morphology here, and 는 remains the only pronounced subject particle. T's edge requirement then triggers Internal Merge of the entire topic-marked subject from the little-v edge shown in the preceding workspace. The new occurrence occupies the finite subject position, while the thematic occurrence is retained as a silent copy. The movement relation also establishes higher-copy pronunciation, transferring the existing 민수는 realization to the new occurrence without changing its morphological composition. The tense exponent 았 is present, but association with the complete token 않았다 waits until the declarative ending is introduced.
derivationStages.statement: Merge past tense, license the subject, and raise it to the finite subject position.

relations.relation: topic Internal Merge and copy pronunciation

values.movement: A-bar movement to the topic edge
values.pronunciation: clause-edge occurrence pronounced; finite and thematic occurrences silent

values.interpretation: Minsu is the topic of the negative past-tense proposition

values.operation: suffixal realization without syntactic head movement

derivationStages.stageRecord: A silent topic head merges with the finite constituent. Its topic feature attracts the topic-marked subject from the finite subject position established in the preceding stage. Internal Merge creates the clause-edge occurrence and leaves the finite occurrence silent, so only the highest member of the subject chain is pronounced. The topic dependency connects this highest occurrence with the silent topic head and makes the proposition about Minsu; contrastive use of the same topic marking does not require another structure. The declarative head 다 then merges above the topic constituent. Finally, morphological realization associates the negative auxiliary 않, past 았, and declarative 다 with 않았다. This is suffixal realization across the extended verbal projection, not an unrecorded syntactic head-movement derivation. The completed structure has past tense above long-form negation and expresses that, as for Minsu, he did not give a book or books to Younghee. The bare noun's number and definiteness remain contextually determined rather than being encoded by additional alternative trees. The supplied terminal period is orthographic punctuation, not an additional indexed token.
derivationStages.statement: Complete the topic dependency and declarative clause, and realize the finite negative auxiliary.

derivationStages.stageRecord: The analysis treats this sentence as a topic-marked subject with a dative recipient, an accusative theme, and Korean long-form negation. External Merge combines each proper-name or nominal D object with its following particle. The resulting head-final objects are labeled K because their particle heads determine their category. The subject's 는 expresses topic marking, not an additional thematic role. First, 민수 and 는 jointly receive the input association 민수는; second, 영희 and 에게 jointly receive 영희에게; third, 책 and 을 jointly receive 책을. These associations retain the noun and particle as separate syntactic terminals. The remaining selected objects are the lexical verb 주, a silent event-introducing v, nonfinite 지, negative auxiliary 않, past 았, and declarative 다. Projection labels throughout identify the projecting head rather than introducing separate bar-level categories.
derivationStages.statement: Select the lexical material and build the three particle-marked nominal objects.

derivationStages.stageRecord: External Merge first combines 주 with the accusative theme 책을, then merges the dative recipient 영희에게 above that combination. The resulting head-final V structure places the recipient before the theme and the verb. The first thematic relation identifies 책을 as the transferred theme of 주; the second identifies 영희에게 as its recipient. The silent v then merges with this V object, and 민수는 merges at the edge of the resulting v structure. The third thematic relation identifies this lower subject occurrence as the agent introduced by v. Topic marking does not prevent the nominal from receiving the agent role. This analysis uses direct V-level introduction of the recipient rather than an additional applicative head; the input does not require an overt applicative distinction.
derivationStages.statement: Build the giving predicate and merge its external argument.

derivationStages.stageRecord: External Merge places the nonfinite head 지 after the completed v object. Here 지 heads a deficient, non-phase-forming complement: it neither introduces another subject nor creates an opaque finite clause. This commitment permits the single subject to participate in the later finite dependency across the negative auxiliary. The newly established realization dependency connects the lexical verb 주 with 지, jointly associating them with 주지. No syntactic head movement is posited merely to construct this written word; the intervening v is silent, and the grouping records the realization of the retained separate terminals.
derivationStages.statement: Form the nonfinite complement required by long-form negation.

values.licensing: structural subject licensing compatible with overt topic marking

derivationStages.stageRecord: External Merge combines the 지 complement with the negative auxiliary 않. The first relation records that this auxiliary negates the giving predication, rather than forming constituent negation of either nominal argument. Past T then merges above the negative auxiliary structure, placing past tense outside negation. The second relation establishes abstract finite licensing between T and the existing lower subject 민수는. This is not a claim of overt person or number agreement in Korean: it supplies the subject's finite syntactic licensing while 는 remains its pronounced topic marker. The auxiliary introduces no additional thematic subject. Because the 지 complement is deficient in this analysis, it does not block this dependency. The final finite word is not yet associated with 않았다 because declarative 다 has not yet joined this structure.
derivationStages.statement: Introduce negative scope and finite tense above the nonfinite predicate.

relations.relation: Subject Internal Merge and copy pronunciation

values.dependency: A-movement to the edge of finite T
values.pronunciation: higher copy pronounced; lower copy silent

derivationStages.stageRecord: Internal Merge copies the already present lower subject to the edge of T. The movement relation connects these exact two occurrences; the higher copy is pronounced and the lower copy, including its noun and particle, is silent. The subject's token association consequently belongs to the higher copy, while its agent interpretation remains grounded in the lower position. This analysis realizes the initial topic as a topic-marked grammatical subject, without positing a separate hanging-topic clause or an additional silent resumptive pronoun. Declarative 다 then externally merges above T. Finally, the negative auxiliary 않, past 았, and declarative 다 jointly receive the association 않았다. This realization retains their separate syntactic heads and does not require syntactic head movement. The completed head-final structure yields 민수는 영희에게 책을 주지 않았다: a past negative assertion about Minsu giving a book to Yeonghui. Ordinary contextual differences in contrast or focus do not introduce another structural derivation here.
derivationStages.statement: Raise the topic-marked subject and complete the declarative clause.

examples.sentence: A könyvet csak Anna olvasta el.

derivationStages.stageRecord: The clause means 'Only Anna read the book,' with el contributing a completive reading. In this X-bar/GB analysis, the subject is base-generated in Spec-IP and receives the external theta-role through predication; a VP-internal subject position is therefore not additionally posited. The verb selects the definite object DP A könyvet as its complement. The particle el occupies Spec-VP, giving the particle–verb order that would characterize a neutral clause without identificational focus. First, olvasta assigns Agent to csak Anna and Theme to A könyvet. Second, its association with el supplies the completive interpretation. Third, finite I licenses nominative Case on the subject. Fourth, V governs and assigns accusative Case to the object, overtly marked on könyvet. Finally, the inflected lexical verb is licensed by past-tense I, third-person singular subject agreement, and the definite conjugation associated with the definite object. Olvasta is introduced as a whole inflected word; the silent I head contains grammatical features, not a separately pronounced suffix. Within the subject DP, csak is an adjoined focus-sensitive particle, and Anna is represented as a proper-name D. The workspace is a base structure, not yet the pronounced word order.
derivationStages.statement: Establish the argument structure, preverbal particle, and finite clause before displacement.

values.dependency: local head chain with a governed V trace

derivationStages.stageRecord: Olvasta moves from the V position displayed in the preceding workspace and adjoins to finite I. The resulting complex I head contains the pronounced verb and the silent tense head; a silent head trace replaces the verb in its theta-assigning position. This local V-to-I dependency links the raised verb to its governed trace and preserves the object's theta-role and accusative licensing at the base position. Because el is a phrasal specifier rather than an intervening head, it does not block this head movement and does not accompany the verb. This intermediate workspace is recorded because the later movement to the focus head takes the already formed finite head as its source. No additional morphological segmentation or change in the pronunciation of olvasta is assumed.
derivationStages.statement: Raise the inflected verb to I while leaving the particle inside VP.

values.licensing: theta-role and accusative Case retained through the object chain
Agent theta-role and nominative Case retained through the subject chain

values.interpretation: Anna, and no relevant alternative to Anna, read the book to completion

derivationStages.stageRecord: The left periphery is projected as CP above TopP above FocP above IP, with silent declarative C, topic, and focus heads. First, A könyvet moves from the previously displayed complement of V to Spec-TopP, leaving an A-bar trace in its Case-marked, theta-marked position. It is interpreted as the discourse topic, approximately 'as for the book'; no resumptive pronoun or independently base-generated left-dislocated DP is posited. Second, the complete DP csak Anna moves from Spec-IP to Spec-FocP, leaving a subject trace. The focus and topic chains each connect a c-commanding antecedent with its local trace and preserve the argument licensing established below. Third, csak is associated with Anna as its alternative-bearing restriction and takes the clause's predicate, with the topic interpreted through its object trace, as its scope. Thus the claim excludes relevant alternatives to Anna as readers of the book. The entire modified subject, rather than Anna alone, occupies the single preverbal focus position. The finite head is still in I in this intermediate structure: the next operation must move that existing head to Foc.
derivationStages.statement: Establish the object topic and the exclusive preverbal subject focus.

values.dependency: successive local head movement from V through I to Foc
values.motivation: identificational focus requires the finite verb in Foc

derivationStages.stageRecord: The complex finite head moves intact from the I position shown in the preceding stage and adjoins to Foc, leaving a silent I trace. This extends the verb's head-movement dependency through the immediately intervening finite head rather than moving V directly across I. The movement satisfies the focus head's requirement for the finite verb and places olvasta immediately after csak Anna. The particle el remains in Spec-VP: its postverbal position results from verb movement, not from an independent rightward movement of the particle. Although evacuation of the subject had already made the pronounced focus and I linearly adjacent in the previous intermediate workspace, the present operation establishes their required structural Spec–head configuration. The completed clause therefore has an object topic, an exclusive subject focus, and a finite verb raised across the stranded particle. The argument traces remain locally antecedent-governed within their respective A-bar chains, and the head traces form the successive V–I–Foc dependency. There is no additional pronominal binding or control dependency in this sentence. The pronounced terminals now give exactly A könyvet csak Anna olvasta el.
derivationStages.statement: Complete focus-triggered head movement and derive the exact surface order.

examples.sentence: A könyvet csak Anna olvasta el.

relations.relation: Internal theta-role and accusative Case assignment

derivationStages.stageRecord: The verb olvasta is inserted as a whole inflected word: past tense, third-person singular, and definite conjugation. Its internal argument is the accusative DP A könyvet, with A as determiner and könyvet as the noun; the overt accusative ending remains inside the lexical word. The verb assigns this DP the Theme role and accusative Case. The verbal particle el occupies the preverbal particle position, represented here as Spec-VP. Its aspectual contribution combines with the reading predicate to give the completed-reading interpretation of elolvas. This is a verbal particle, not a preposition requiring an unexpressed complement. Separately, the subject DP is constructed with csak as an exclusive modifier of the proper-name DP Anna. The proper name has an unpronounced determiner. A silent finite T bears the features corresponding to the already inflected verb. These are lexicalist GB commitments: the input words are not split into independently pronounced inflectional terminals.
derivationStages.statement: Construct the lexical predicate and the subject expression.

derivationStages.stageRecord: T takes VP as its complement, and the subject DP merges in Spec-TP. This analysis uses the classical GB external-subject configuration rather than a VP-internal subject: the reading predicate assigns its external Agent role to the subject in Spec-TP. Finite T licenses nominative Case on that DP. Anna has no overt nominative suffix, which is compatible with Hungarian nominative marking. The exclusive modifier remains part of the subject DP, so the entire expression csak Anna can subsequently move as one constituent. At this point the object is still the verb's complement and el remains in its preverbal base position.
derivationStages.statement: Establish the finite clause and the subject's argument position.

derivationStages.stageRecord: The verb moves from V to T by head adjunction, leaving an unpronounced V-trace in its earlier position. The resulting complex T contains the pronounced verb and the silent tense head. This first head-movement step is recorded separately because the later movement to Foc must originate in this established T position. The verb's lexical past-tense, third-person singular, and definite-conjugation features are licensed against finite T, the subject, and the definite object. No spelling change or word fusion occurs: olvasta remains one input word. The particle does not accompany the verb, and the object remains in the complement position.
derivationStages.statement: Raise the lexical verb to finite T.

values.interpretation: Anna, and no other relevant alternative, read the book to completion

derivationStages.stageRecord: A FocP is projected above TP, and the whole subject DP moves from Spec-TP to Spec-FocP, leaving an unpronounced DP-trace. This is A′-movement: the subject's Agent role and nominative Case remain associated with its lower argument position. The exclusive modifier csak is carried with Anna rather than stranded. The focused DP and the focus head establish the narrow subject-focus configuration: among the contextually relevant alternatives, Anna alone satisfies the completed-reading predicate. The focus head is still unpronounced and the finite verb remains in T in this intermediate workspace. This intermediate state makes the subject's focus placement available before the focus-driven head movement.
derivationStages.statement: Move csak Anna into the preverbal focus position.

values.configuration: focused subject in Spec-FocP with the finite verb in Foc

derivationStages.stageRecord: The complex finite T head now moves from its established T position and adjoins to Foc. Its earlier T position becomes an unpronounced head trace; the lexical V-trace remains lower in VP. The pronounced verb therefore immediately follows the focused subject. Because el stays in Spec-VP, it follows the raised verb instead of preceding it. This derives the sentence-specific sequence csak Anna olvasta el. The postverbal particle is thus a consequence of focus-driven verb raising, not a particle that has itself moved rightward. The focused subject and the raised finite head satisfy the Hungarian preverbal focus configuration.

The object retains the Theme role and accusative Case established in its base position; this is topicalization, not passive promotion. A silent declarative C completes the root CP. The subject and object A′-chains connect each fronted DP to its argument trace, permitting interpretation at the theta-marked positions. The intervening subject trace is not an A′-binder of the object trace, and neither extraction crosses an embedded finite clause. The head chain connects the pronounced verb in Foc to its T and V traces. No PRO or resumptive pronoun is posited, and Anna is an unbound referential expression, compatible with Binding Principle C. The resulting pronounced order is exactly A könyvet csak Anna olvasta el. The completed reading is 'As for the book, only Anna read it to completion.'
